title: Spreadsheet formulas
examples: When should I use the IF function in a spreadsheet?
What is the difference between $A$1 and A1 in formulas?
Can you show me how to sum a range of cells correctly?

explain.say: Today we learn key spreadsheet formulas for data analysis.

items: SUM adds up a range of numbers.
IF checks a condition and gives an outcome.
References lock or unlock cell locations.

explain.say: The SUM function adds up many numbers in a selected group.
The IF function checks if something is true or false.
Relative references change when you copy the formula.
Absolute references use dollar signs to keep cells fixed.
Real life example: Calculating commission rates.

faq.q: How do I sum numbers that are not in a neat column?
faq.a: You can select the non-adjacent cells and list them inside the SUM function parentheses. For example, you would use equals SUM open parenthesis cell A1 comma cell C5 comma cell F10 close parenthesis.
asks: What if I want to add A1 and C5?

faq.q: What is the structure of an IF statement?
faq.a: The IF function always requires three parts: the logical test, what to show if it passes, and what to show if it fails. Remember the structure is equals IF open parenthesis test comma true value comma false value close parenthesis.
asks: How do I write a simple pass fail check?

faq.q: When should I use an absolute reference?
faq.a: Use absolute references when a cell value must remain the same regardless of where you copy the formula. This is common when using a fixed tax rate across many calculations.
asks: When is $ needed in a formula?
What stops a reference from changing?

faq.q: What is the difference between relative and absolute references?
faq.a: Relative references adjust automatically when copied, like moving across a grid. Absolute references lock the row and column using dollar signs, keeping them fixed.
asks: Which reference changes when I drag the formula?
How do I lock a cell reference?

faq.a: Yes, you can nest IF statements to check multiple conditions in sequence. You simply place a new IF statement into the 'valueiffalse' argument of the previous IF.
asks: What if I need to check three or more conditions?

facts: The SUM function syntax is equals SUM open parenthesis range close parenthesis.
The IF function syntax requires three arguments: test, true, false.
A relative reference like A1 changes when the formula is copied.
An absolute reference like $A$1 locks both the column and the row.

quiz.say: To sum the values in cells B2 through B10, what is the correct formula?
quiz.why: The colon indicates a continuous range, so B2 through B10 is correct for summing.

wrong.1: This only adds the values in B2 and B10, skipping the rest.
wrong.2: This only adds two cells, not the entire range between them.
wrong.3: Formulas must begin with an equals sign to be calculated.

quiz.say: If a student scores 50, and the passing mark is 60, what IF formula determines 'Pass' or 'Fail'?
quiz.why: The test checks if A1 is greater than or equal to 60, and returns 'Pass' if true.

wrong.1: This only checks for exactly 60, not scores above it.
wrong.2: The test condition must include the comparison operator like >=.
wrong.3: This misses students who score exactly 60, who should pass.
